lead.headline: Apple takes Steve Jobs to court over his new computer venture
lead.dek: A $5-million suit turns the cofounder’s new venture into a legal battleground.
body: Apple sued Steve Jobs on September 23, escalating the dispute surrounding its departed cofounder and his new computer venture. The Los Angeles Times reports the action in its September 24 edition under a headline describing a $5-million lawsuit.

Jobs has recruited five Apple employees for the new company. Apple’s complaint concerns alleged use of insider information: those accusations are claims in a dispute, not findings that wrongdoing has occurred.

The new venture’s machine specifications are not yet finished. There is no finished workstation to put on a shop counter, and readers should not mistake the personnel battle for a product introduction.

For personal-computer buyers, the immediate story is the split itself: a major manufacturer and the entrepreneur who helped build it now face one another across a legal divide. The new company’s eventual computer remains a question for another issue.

stories.headline: Lucasfilm’s delayed games reach Atari owners through Epyx
body: Lucasfilm’s Rescue on Fractalus! and Ballblazer receive an enthusiastic Atari review from Tom R. Halfhill in September COMPUTE!. The magazine coverage gives players a close look at two delayed games rather than establishing a new release date this week.

Rescue on Fractalus! sends the pilot over fractal terrain on a rescue mission. Ballblazer trades that landscape for split-screen futuristic soccer, with two players or a computer opponent. The reviewed Atari versions require 48K, a disk drive and a joystick; a second stick is recommended for Ballblazer.

The listed Epyx price is $40 apiece. The games’ original Atari connection became entangled in Atari’s business troubles before Epyx secured marketing rights. Apple II and Commodore 64 versions remain pending in this review; the C64 Ballblazer is still in development.

stories.headline: Amiga review makes the case for a multimedia personal computer
body: September COMPUTE! devotes a substantial pre-release review to the Amiga, treating it as a personal computer with ambitions stretching well beyond a single application. Tom R. Halfhill explores games, business, education, video art and electronic music.

The appeal is the combination: a machine that can make graphics and sound central to everyday computing rather than optional decorations. Halfhill’s comparisons with costlier business and dedicated graphics equipment are the reviewer’s assessments, not independent benchmark results.

The review follows the summer New York introduction and repeats Commodore’s expectation of availability by the end of August. A forecast in a pre-release review does not establish which shops have stock during this September week.

stories.headline: Atari’s ST roadmap promises cheaper machines and compact-disc storage
body: September Antic surveys Atari ST plans first announced at June’s Consumer Electronics Show. The proposed 256K 260ST is priced at $399, with a 260STD incorporating a 3.5-inch drive proposed at $499; the report targets October or November.

ROM-resident GEM/TOS and built-in television RF modulation are among the promised changes. These are announcements, not confirmation that the machines have arrived. A $799 520ST package with monochrome monitor and disk drive provides a more concrete comparison in the report.

Storage and communications also figure in the roadmap: a proposed 500-megabyte CD-ROM system, plus Haba’s promised $499 10-megabyte hard disk and $299 Hayes-compatible modem. Availability and final specifications still need checking before a buyer spends the money.

worldAnchor.headline: Hurricane Gloria strikes the East Coast
worldAnchor.summary: On September 27 Gloria crossed North Carolina’s Outer Banks and continued north. National Weather Service retrospective verifies the event; avoid importing later damage totals into a contemporaneous bulletin.

bbsNote.headline: SIG wars: online communities become competitive assets
bbsNote.summary: Arlan R. Levitan’s September COMPUTE! column reports earlier events, including May’s short-lived Delphi MAUG branch; use as same-month commentary, not a new September shutdown. Antic documents the practical appeal of CompuServe’s Atari library.

posts.text: Reported by COMPUTE!, not an actual recovered BBS post: Delphi’s MAUG branch vanished after a few weeks and was replaced by a generic Apple SIG; CompuServe’s MAUG developed separate Apple II, Macintosh and developer forums.
Levitan reports Delphi off-shift 1200-bps access cost half CompuServe’s comparable charge; even Delphi’s 2400-bps off-shift rate was lower. No absolute hourly rate verified.
Jerry White credits sysop Richard Brudaynski and members with recommendations from a library exceeding 1,000 programs. Downloads were not separately charged beyond normal service access time.

curiosity.headline: Your television can schedule the lamps
curiosity.summary: General Electric’s HomeMinder turns the TV into a pictorial home-control interface.
curiosity.detail: David H. Ahl’s September Creative Computing evaluation describes control over existing house wiring, a stand-alone controller or a version built into a 25-inch TV, and up to 96 on/off times per controlled unit. Touch-tone telephone access can control devices and leave short messages. This is a review, not a verified launch this week.

gadgetWatch.headline: GE HomeMinder brings home automation to the television
gadgetWatch.summary: September review describes remote-controlled lights, appliances and heating/cooling using existing wiring, with television setup menus and telephone access. No retail price verified.
